readerTitle: "Send me something" is not a yes
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 업체, 포장재 제조사) + 실제 연구 (Neil Rackham, SPIN Selling)
insight: 클로징은 마지막에 한 번 쓰는 기술이 아니라, 대화를 마칠 때마다 고객이 할 수 있는 구체적인 다음 행동을 요청하는 일이다.
misconception: 클로징은 계약 직전에 쓰는 압박 기술이다. 좋은 제품은 굳이 요청하지 않아도 팔린다.

sources.text: Rackham, N. (1988). SPIN Selling. McGraw-Hill. (Huthwaite의 영업 상담 연구, advance와 continuation 구분, 대형 거래에서 클로징 기법의 효과)
청소 업체와 포장재 제조사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Rackham 연구의 규모(흔히 '12년간 약 35,000건의 상담'으로 인용됨)는 카드에 숫자로 쓰지 않고 'a large study of sales calls'로만 적었습니다. 원문으로 규모를 확인하세요.
'압박형 클로징 기법이 소액 거래에서는 도움이 되지만 대형 거래에서는 성공률을 낮췄다'는 요지가 SPIN Selling 원문(클로징 관련 장)과 맞는지 확인하세요. 구체적인 비율은 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
advance(고객이 거래를 앞으로 진전시키는 행동에 동의)와 continuation(구체적 약속 없이 대화가 끝남)의 정의가 Rackham의 표현과 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The meeting went great. Then nothing.
body: Maya runs a commercial cleaning company. She meets an office manager who nods through the whole pitch. At the end he smiles: "This sounds great. Send me something."
She sends a proposal that night. Three weeks and two follow-up emails later, she has heard nothing. Nobody said no. The deal just stopped moving.

image.label: A salesperson waiting by a silent phone next to a sent proposal
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 업체 사장이 책상에 앉아 조용한 휴대폰을 바라보고 있고, 화면에는 'Sent' 표시된 제안서 이메일. 벽 달력에 3주가 X로 지워져 있음. 실제 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rewind to the end of the meeting.
body: The office manager says, "This sounds good, send me something." You have about thirty seconds before he walks you out.

options.feedback: Fast and friendly, and the proposal gets sent. But nothing is agreed: no date, no reply expected, and you don't know who actually decides.

options.text: "If you sign by Friday, I can take 10% off the first month."
options.feedback: It creates urgency, but it costs margin and can feel like pressure from someone he met an hour ago. He may still not be the one who signs.

options.text: "Happy to. Who else needs to see it? Could we book 20 minutes on Thursday to walk through it together?"
options.feedback: You ask for a small, specific step he can say yes to today. You also learn who decides and get a date on the calendar.

cards.title: "Send me something" is a polite goodbye.
body: Often it means "this was nice, and I'd like the meeting to end." The proposal then lands with someone who may not decide, with no time set to discuss it.

Maya's deal didn't fail at the price or the service. It failed in the last minute of the meeting, because **nobody agreed to do anything next**. Silence felt kinder than a no, so silence is what she got.

cards.title: Closing
body: **Closing** means asking the customer for a clear commitment they are ready to make. Often that is the signature. Often it is just the next step: a meeting with the boss, a site visit, a trial.
Seen this way, closing doesn't happen once at the end of a sale. It happens at the end of every conversation, in small steps that keep the sale moving.

image.label: A staircase of small commitments leading to a signed contract
image.brief: 계단 인포그래픽. 아래부터 'Intro call', 'Site visit', 'Meet the decision maker', 'Trial', 맨 위 'Signed'. 각 계단에 작은 달력 아이콘과 날짜. 계단 옆 바닥에 흐릿한 'Let's keep in touch' 말풍선이 멈춰 있음.

cards.title: Advances beat clever closes.
body: In the 1970s and 80s, researcher Neil Rackham and his team at Huthwaite ran a large study of real sales calls. He published the results in *SPIN Selling* (1988).
He split call endings into two kinds. An **advance**: the customer agrees to an action that moves the sale forward. A *continuation*: the call ends warmly, but with no specific commitment.
He also reported that classic pressure closes tended to help in small, cheap sales but hurt results in larger ones. Big buyers resisted being pushed. They responded to clear, reasonable next steps.

cards.eyebrow: What a good ask looks like
cards.title: Specific, active, dated.
body: A strong next step has three parts:
list: **Specific:** "a tasting of three samples," not "let's talk more"
**The customer does something:** shows up, brings a colleague, shares data
**It has a date:** "next Tuesday at 10," not "soon"
cards.callout: A bakery supplier asks for a tasting. A kitchen remodeler asks to measure on Saturday. Same move.
cards.softwareNote: For a software product, "I'll start a free trial" is often a continuation in disguise. A real advance is "let's set it up with your own data on a call Wednesday."

cards.title: You can only ask for what you've earned.
body: Asking for a contract after one chat feels pushy because it is. The size of the ask should match how much the customer already understands and trusts you. That work happens in qualifying and discovery, not in the last minute.
And a clear no is a good outcome. It frees your time for customers who might say yes. Tricks that squeeze out a yes today can cost you the repeat business and referrals tomorrow.

cards.title: Now you make packaging.
body: Your factory makes cardboard boxes. A food producer's buyer has toured your plant and liked the samples. As you walk out, she says: "We'll need to think about it."

options.text: "Of course. Call me whenever you're ready."
options.feedback: Polite and low-pressure, but it's a pure continuation. You hand all the timing to her and never learn what she's unsure about.

options.text: "What would you need to see to decide? Could we run a trial batch on your packing line next week, with your production lead there?"
options.feedback: You uncover the real concern and propose a step that tests it. A trial with her production lead also brings the next decision maker into the room.

options.text: "If you order this month, I'll take 10% off the first run."
options.feedback: It might speed things up, but you give away margin without knowing what's holding her back. If the worry is quality on her line, a discount won't fix it.

cards.softwareNote: The same applies when a software buyer says "we'll think about it" after a demo: ask what they'd need to see, then offer a pilot with the team that will use it daily.

cards.title: Never end a conversation without a next step.
body: Closing isn't a trick at the finish line. It's asking, every time, for a specific step the customer is ready to take, with a date.
**Try it today:** look at your three most promising open deals. For each, write down the next agreed step and its date. If you can't, that's your next call.
